title: How to Run a Support Group Online: A Complete Guide
summary: Can an online support group really work? What changes when you move a group to video, what breaks, and how to keep people coming back.
body_markdown:
An online group is not an in-person group on a screen. Some of what makes a room work survives the move and some of it does not, and the parts that do not have to be rebuilt deliberately.


This is what actually changes, what tends to break, and what holds a virtual group together over months rather than weeks.


## What online gains you


- **Geography stops mattering.** A group for a rare diagnosis, or for a specific and narrow experience, becomes possible when you are drawing from a region or a country rather than a neighborhood.
- **The people who could never come, can.** Carers who cannot leave the house, people with limited mobility, shift workers, parents without childcare, anyone for whom an hour of travel each way was the barrier.
- **Attendance is steadier.** Weather, transport and a bad day are much smaller obstacles when the meeting is in the next room.
- **Anonymity is easier.** For subjects people are not ready to be seen with locally, this is decisive.


MentalHappy hosts expert-led psychoeducational support groups online, supplemental to professional care rather than a replacement for it. Nothing on the platform is therapy or treatment.


## What online costs you, and what to do about it


### You lose the edges of the meeting


In a room, the ten minutes before and after the session are where a great deal of the connection actually happens. Online, people arrive at the exact minute and vanish at the end.


Open the call ten minutes early and stay on for ten after, and say that you do. Most weeks two or three people will use it. That is the equivalent of the corridor, and it matters more than it sounds.


### You lose ambient reading of the room


You cannot see who has gone still, who is holding back tears, who has quietly checked out. A gallery of faces at postage-stamp size is not the same information.


Compensate by making state explicit. A one-word check-in at the start and a one-word close at the end gives you a reading you would otherwise have got for free. Ask people to keep cameras on where they can, but make it a request rather than a rule, for some members, camera-off is the only way they attend at all.


### Silence becomes unreadable


In a room, a pause has texture. Online, three seconds of nothing feels like a technical failure, so facilitators fill it and members stop trying to speak.


Name it once, early: *Online, silence feels longer than it is. I'm going to leave gaps on purpose.* Then leave them. Count to ten.


### Interruption is harder


Video calls punish overlap, so people stop trying, and the two most confident members end up holding the session.


Go round deliberately for check-ins rather than leaving it open. Use the chat as a second channel, "drop a word in the chat" gets contributions from people who will not unmute. And name the quiet ones into the conversation gently rather than waiting for them to find a gap that never comes.


### The group disappears between sessions


An in-person group leaves traces: the people you saw, the room you went to. An online group vanishes entirely the moment the call ends.


This is the single biggest reason virtual groups lose people. Something has to exist between sessions: a group space where people can post, a short message from you a day before each session, a shared thread where members drop one thing that helped.


## The practical setup


- **Same day, same time, same link.** A changing link is a lost member. Send it in the same form every week.
- **Sixty to ninety minutes.** Online attention fades faster than in a room; ninety is a genuine ceiling.
- **Six to twelve people.** Above twelve, a video call stops being a conversation and becomes a broadcast.
- **A reminder the day before.** Two lines and the link. Nothing changes attendance more.
- **Waiting room on, and you admit people.** This is your door, and a group without one is not private.


### What to look for in a platform


The questions that matter are not about video quality. They are: can someone join from a phone without a complicated install, can the group be private and invitation-only, can you send reminders without giving out your personal number, is there a space that persists between sessions, and can you moderate (remove, mute, disable chat) while a session is live. A general video tool does the call; it does not do the membership, the reminders or the between-session space.


## Running the session itself


1. **Open early, admit people by name.** Being greeted by name at the door does most of the work of arriving.
2. **Housekeeping in thirty seconds.** Recording (don't), cameras (preference not rule), chat (how you use it), what to do if you drop out.
3. **One-word check-in, everyone, in order.** Do not skip this because it seems mechanical. It gets every voice into the room in the first five minutes, which makes speaking later dramatically easier.
4. **The main conversation.** Go round explicitly rather than leaving the floor open. Leave gaps.
5. **One-word close, everyone, in order.** Then confirm the next date before anyone leaves.
6. **Stay on for ten minutes.** Say you will.


Two habits that pay off disproportionately: say people's names constantly, and read the chat aloud. Online, an unacknowledged contribution feels much more ignored than it would in a room.


## When something goes wrong


Decide in advance and it is a two-minute problem rather than the thing that ends the group.


- **Someone becomes distressed.** Slow down, speak to them directly, and do not leave them alone on the call at the end. Have a helpline number and two local services written down before you need them.
- **Someone dominates.** Acknowledge, summarize, hand on. *That's a lot to be carrying. Has anyone else been sitting with something like that?*
- **Someone behaves badly.** Mute or remove. Then follow up privately. Doing this quickly is protective of everyone else, and hesitating is what members remember.
- **Your connection drops.** Tell the group in advance what happens if the host disappears, usually: wait five minutes, then the session is over and you will message them.


Do not record sessions. The chilling effect on what people are willing to say is larger than any benefit, and the storage of it is a problem you do not want.


## Questions about running online


### Do online support groups actually work?


For many people, yes, and for some they work better than in-person groups, because they remove travel, widen who can attend and make anonymity easier. What they require is more deliberate facilitation: silence, disengagement and distress are all harder to read on a screen.


### How long should an online support group session be?


Sixty to ninety minutes. Attention drops faster on video than in a room, and ninety minutes is a real ceiling for most groups. Keep the length fixed so people can plan around it.


### Should members keep their cameras on?


Ask, but do not require it. Cameras on makes facilitating far easier, and for some members camera-off is the only way they attend at all. Make it a stated preference with an explicit exception rather than a rule people have to break.


### What platform should I use for an online support group?


Look past video quality. The things that matter are joining from a phone without a difficult install, invitation-only privacy, reminders you can send without sharing your personal number, a space that persists between sessions, and live moderation controls. A general video-conferencing tool covers only the call.


### Should I record the sessions?


No. Recording changes what people are willing to say, and storing recordings of sensitive conversations creates a risk you do not need. If someone misses a session, a short written summary of themes with no personal detail is a better answer.
